For instance, "She seemed happy," suggests that she appeared to be happy, but it doesn't necessarily mean that she was truly happy. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** __ • **Perhaps**: This is an adverb that indicates uncertainty or possibility. It is used when you are not certain about something. For example, in the sentence, "Perhaps it will rain later," the speaker is suggesting that it might rain later, but they aren't sure. • **Besides**: This can function as a preposition or an adverb. As a preposition, it means 'in addition to' or 'apart from'. For example, "Besides basketball, she also plays tennis," meaning she plays tennis in addition to basketball. As an adverb, it can mean 'moreover' or 'also'. For example, "I don't want to go to the party. Besides, I have to study," where 'besides' introduces an additional reason. • **Thought**: This is the past tense of the verb "think," which means to have a particular belief or idea. It also refers to the act or process of considering, believing, or remembering something. For example, "I thought you were going to the store," suggests that the speaker previously believed that the other person was going to the store. questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
questions.solution:

The word "who" is used as the subject of a sentence or clause, and it refers to a person. In this case, the sentence is likely asking for the subject of a verb or the person who is performing an action. For example, "Who is going to the party?" or "Who wrote this book?"

Option 2, "whose," is used to show possession or ownership. For example, "Whose car is this?" or "Whose idea was it to go on this trip?"

Option 3, "whom," is used as the object of a sentence or clause, and it refers to a person. For example, "Whom did you invite to the party?" or "To whom should I address this letter?"

Option 4, "which," is used to refer to things or objects. For example, "Which book do you want to read?" or "Which color do you prefer?"

Additional Information:
It's important to note that the use of "whom" is becoming less common in modern English, and many people use "who" instead, even in formal writing. However, in very formal or academic writing, "whom" may still be preferred.
